regional_origin: Island-wide (especially upcountry, where fresh fish was historically scarce)

ingredients.name: Dried salted fish (katta karawala)
ingredients.notes: soaked in water for 30-40 minutes to remove excess salt and any sand/impurities, then drained and cut into pieces

ingredients.name: Banana pepper or green bell pepper
Potato
ingredients.notes: optional, small, cut into cubes, to bulk out the dish

steps.instruction: Rinse the dried fish, then soak in water for 30-40 minutes to remove the excess salt layer and any sand or impurities from the drying process. Drain and squeeze out the water, then cut into bite-sized pieces.
In a pot, combine the soaked dried fish with the onion, garlic, green chillies, tomato, banana pepper (if using), potato (if using), curry leaves, black peppercorns, turmeric, and chilli powder.
Add the water. Cover and cook on medium-low heat for about 10-12 minutes, until the dried fish softens and the tomato breaks down, stirring occasionally.
Pour in the coconut milk. Stir well and bring to a gentle simmer over low heat, cooking for a further 5-8 minutes -- avoid boiling vigorously, as this can curdle the coconut milk.
Taste the curry before adding any salt -- the dried fish is usually salty enough on its own, and most cooks find no extra salt is needed. Add a small pinch only if truly necessary.
Turn off the heat, let cool slightly, and stir in the lime juice. Serve hot with rice, string hoppers, or coconut roti, alongside coconut sambol to balance the saltiness.

source_site: hungrylankan.com, cross-checked against rasakama.wordpress.com, pulse.lk, and foodcnr.com for technique and salt-handling consistency
collection_method: scraped, cross-checked across 5+ independent sources; very strong agreement on the salt-removal soak as the essential first step
notes: Dried fish (karawala) was historically a preservation method allowing fish to be transported and eaten in upcountry areas without refrigeration, and remains a beloved comfort food, especially paired with pol sambol (sl_016) and rice. The pre-soak is the single most important step in this recipe -- skipping it results in an unpleasantly over-salty dish, and dried fish can also carry sand or grit from open-air drying that needs rinsing away. The variety used here is 'katta karawala', a popular type for curries, but other dried fish varieties (including dried anchovies/Maldive fish-style small fish) can substitute. A completely different, oil-fried version called 'karawala thel dala' (dry fish fry, no coconut milk) is a separate, equally popular preparation not covered by this entry. No salt is listed as an ingredient since nearly all sources agree the dish's own saltiness from the dried fish is sufficient.
